transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-09
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Amira Patel (Sable), Jon Reeves (Sable), Leila Morgan (Sable)
---
Auto-summary (AI): Walkthrough of curation sprint — selecting candidate open models, running persona benchmarks, reading compatibility matrices, then building a runbook that maps to kernel/hardware choices and routing fallbacks. Action: schedule pilot and deliver bench spreadsheet.

00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we're gonna run through the curation sprint, uh, show the catalog views and then dig into the bench interpretation, and the runbook that comes out of it.
00:28 Amira Patel: Thanks Maya. Quick note — Jon's gonna keep an eye on infra questions, Leila's focusing on product metrics. We're hoping to pick a short-list and start a pilot in mid-April.
00:45 Carlos Ruiz: Awesome. I can jump in on the bench side and the kernel mapping. Quick question — do you want me to assume our workload is mostly chat generation with 1–2k context?
01:10 Leila Morgan: Yes, roughly. Most queries are 256–1024 tokens, few long docs for retrieval. Latency is important; cost is also a hard constraint.
01:35 Maya Chen: Great. So agenda: catalog filters, priortiza— prioritization heuristics, bench runner, then we'll show generated compatibility matrix and then the runbook template.
02:05 Jon Reeves: Also we need to cover compliance — KMS, audit logs — that's a blocker for our security team.
02:30 Maya Chen: Yep, we'll cover that briefly; we can share the security pack after this meeting.

03:10 Carlos Ruiz: (screenshare) Ok first thing — here's the catalog. You'll notice we tag models by architecture, quantization friendliness, and verified latency profiles. The UI lets you add custom metrics from your bench runs.
03:45 Amira Patel: I see. The tag "quant friendly" — what exactly does that imply in runtime? Does it mean it runs cleanly at 8-bit?
04:05 Carlos Ruiz: Good question. It usually means it was validated across our quantization profiles — but important caveat: some layers still benefit from FP16 kernels. The catalog shows the recommended kernel map per hardware.
04:30 Leila Morgan: Are those kernel mappings deterministic? Like, will the same model always pick the same kernel on the same GPU?
04:55 Carlos Ruiz: Mostly yes, the runtime picks kernels based on model op patterns and sequence distributions; however if you change sequence length or enable some optimizations, the runtime may change the exact kernel set. We include a compatibility matrix so you can see mapping per model/hardware.

06:00 Maya Chen: Now for prioritization — we recommend scoring candidates across criteria: accuracy/bench signal, latency SLO, cost per token, memory footprint, and fallback compatibility. We show a weighted score in the UI.
06:40 Amira Patel: Can we customize weights per route? For example product chat wants low latency, research wants higher quality.
07:00 Maya Chen: Yes; we support route-level profiles so you can tune weights. That also ties into routing policies: you can do latency-first routing or cost-first routing and have automatic fallback to a compatible variant if capacity constrained.

08:20 Carlos Ruiz: Let's look at a bench run. (uploads) Here's a bench with our sample prompts — you'll see columns for rouge/bertscore-ish metrics, perplexity proxy, hallucination checks, and latency p50/p95. Note transcription — sorry, benchmark — some of these metrics are proxies; we explain each.
09:00 Leila Morgan: The hallucination checks — how rigorous are they? We need to know regression risk for customer-facing answers.
09:25 Carlos Ruiz: We run prompt-based evals plus a QA verification tier. We have a regression alerting pipeline tied to prompt sets. During curation sprint you'll iterate on prompts until you hit an acceptable error rate.
09:50 Amira Patel: Do you support custom eval hooks so we can run domain-specific graders?
10:10 Carlos Ruiz: Yes — you can plug in your own grading function, and the bench runner will surface per-model deltas over time.

11:15 Jon Reeves: From infra perspective, curious on the Dedicated offering — if we reserve capacity what are latency SLOs and what's the failover path to hosted?
11:40 Maya Chen: Dedicated is SLA-backed; typical p95 for 512 tokens on our GPU clusters is shown in the catalog profile. We also recommend a fallback policy to route to hosted or quantized variant when Dedicated is saturated — that gives graceful degradation.
12:05 Jon Reeves: And what about private/VPC deployment with HSM? That's a hard req.
12:30 Maya Chen: Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations. We can provide audit logs and longer retention as an add-on. I'll add that to the security docs we share.

13:15 Carlos Ruiz: Ok jumping back to compatibility matrix — here's an example mapping for three candidate models: model-alpha-1, model-beta-3q, and model-gamma-16k. We show which kernels are used on A100 vs H100 vs T4, and approximate memory and perf. Note: some names in the matrix are shorthand, the model registry has canonical ids.
14:00 Leila Morgan: model-beta-3q — is that a 3-bit quant model? The name looks like it. How stable are those models across inputs?
14:25 Carlos Ruiz: 3-bit quant can be a great cost win, but it sometimes increases variance on long-context QA. The bench will surface that; in our prior run we saw a 7% drop in answer accuracy for long context with 3-bit on that family.

15:10 Amira Patel: When you output the runbook, does it include recommended autoscale settings and batching policy?
15:30 Carlos Ruiz: Yes, the runbook template includes suggested batch sizes per model+hardware, KV cache reuse settings, and autoscaler thresholds tuned to keep p95 within your target.
16:00 Maya Chen: We'll also include suggested quant profiles and fallback variants per route.

17:10 (30s of cross talk while screenshare switches)
17:40 Leila Morgan: On the runbook, can product own the route weights or is it infra only?
18:00 Maya Chen: Product can own it via the console — we have RBAC so you can let product teams adjust route profiles without giving infra full cluster access.

19:15 Carlos Ruiz: Now I want to show an annotated bench — here's a case where latency looked fine but a hallucination metric spiked for a specific prompt family. We flagged it, and the curation sprint recommends either prompt fixes or falling back to a higher-quality model for that intent.
20:10 Amira Patel: Helpful. That gives us confidence we'll be able to catch regressions early. Does the bench runner keep history so we can see deltas across deploys?
20:35 Carlos Ruiz: Yes, time series for each metric. You can pin a baseline and the UI shows relative regressions.

21:20 Jon Reeves: A practical ops question — if we run the pilot on our VPC, do you need access to our test images, or can we mount data privately?
21:45 Maya Chen: For VPC/private, data stays in your environment. We supply a small agent to orchestrate bench runs that runs inside your VPC; logs and metrics can be pushed to your monitoring stack or mirrored to our console depending on your policy.

22:30 Leila Morgan: Are the benchmark sample prompts stored anywhere central? We worry about IP and should ensure prompts don't leak.
23:00 Carlos Ruiz: By default they're stored in your account namespace; we recommend encrypting at rest with customer KMS. We can mark prompts and results as private.

24:15 Amira Patel: What's the expected time for an initial curation sprint? From shortlist to runbook?
24:35 Maya Chen: Typically 2–3 weeks for a pragmatic shortlist and initial runbook if you provide initial prompts and sample traffic. Deeper sweeps for more models can add time.

25:00 Carlos Ruiz: Ok here's a decision example — we weight latency 40%, cost 25%, accuracy 25%, memory 10% and run the candidate models. The UI highlights top picks and shows why lower-ranked ones failed (incompatibility on H100 or poor hallucination).
25:40 Leila Morgan: Could we flip to cost-first and see alternate picks real-time?
25:55 Carlos Ruiz: Yep, toggle the profile and it recomputes. The important bit is seeing the compatibility matrix change — some cheap variants are incompatible with your chosen hardware or have no fallback in hosted.

27:00 Amira Patel: On the subject of fallbacks, in case of capacity spike, will request routing maintain session-level consistency for chat conversations?
27:20 Carlos Ruiz: We maintain KV cache awareness. If you route to a different model variant you'll need to ensure the cache is compatible; we provide cross-variant KV compatibility checks and will only route if the target can accept the cached state or we can gracefully rehydrate.

28:10 Jon Reeves: Any precedent for metrics when we blend hosted and dedicated? Concerned about token accounting and cost attribution.
28:35 Maya Chen: Console provides token-level billing and you can attribute routes to projects or cost centers. We also surface estimated per-token cost shifts when routing policies change.

29:20 (short pause)
29:50 Carlos Ruiz: Now I'll step through a sample runbook export — it includes the shortlist, bench summary, recommended model variants, kernel mapping table, autoscale settings, batch sizes, fallback policies, and a checklist for deployment (security checks, data residency affirmations).
30:40 Leila Morgan: That checklist — can you add our SOC 2 cookie-cutter items? We have a vendor checklist that we send around.
31:00 Maya Chen: Yes, we can attach customer-specific compliance artifacts. We'll map your vendor checklist to our security features and flag any gaps.

32:10 Amira Patel: Quick nit — earlier you mentioned the benchmark uses a perplexity proxy; how does that translate to our customer-facing metric of answer correctness?
32:30 Carlos Ruiz: Perplexity is a coarse signal; we prioritize prompt-based QA metrics and hallucination detection for correctness. Perplexity helps triage models quickly but we don't use it as the sole decision metric.

33:20 Jon Reeves: On hardware — do you recommend H100 for our expected load? We're sensitive to p95 during peak hours.
33:40 Carlos Ruiz: H100 gives lower p95 for large models but costs more. For mixed workloads we sometimes pair H100 for high-quality routes and A100 for cost-sensitive routes. The compatibility matrix will show where A100 performs well.

34:50 Leila Morgan: Suppose a model shows marginal improvements in accuracy but triples cost — are there automated guards to prevent accidental routing to expensive variants?
35:10 Maya Chen: Yes — route policies can cap spend per route and refusegoing to variants that exceed cost multipliers; you can set hard caps.

36:00 Carlos Ruiz: Another nuance: kernel mapping can change with model patch versions. Our registry ties kernel recommendations to model version ids so runbook includes the exact model hash used for runs.
36:35 Amira Patel: Great, we need deterministic reproducibility for audits.
36:50 Carlos Ruiz: Exactly.

38:00 (small interruption — phone rings, brief silence)
38:25 Maya Chen: Back — sorry about that. On next steps — we'd like to run a small pilot. Proposal: we run bench jobs against your sample traffic on a 3-model shortlist, produce the runbook, then do a 2-week pilot with Dedicated capacity for one route.
38:55 Amira Patel: Sounds reasonable. Who from Redwood will own the pilot coordination?
39:10 Maya Chen: Carlos will be the SE lead; I'll own commercial and coordinating the pricing.
39:30 Jon Reeves: For the pilot, we'll need a clear roll-back plan and runbook acceptance criteria.
39:45 Carlos Ruiz: We'll include runbook acceptance checklist — runbook must include p95 below X ms for the route, hallucination rate below Y% on the test prompt set, and cost within budget envelope.

41:00 Leila Morgan: How do we measure hallucination rate automatically? Is it manual review?
41:20 Carlos Ruiz: It's a mix — automated QA graders plus a manual review sample. You can increase manual sampling rate for high-risk intents.

42:10 Amira Patel: Any red flags we should be aware of before committing to Dedicated?
42:30 Maya Chen: Major ones are if your model family lacks a compatible quantized variant or if your required compliance features mandate on-prem with long procurement lead times. We surface these early in the sprint.

43:10 Jon Reeves: Procurement question — pricing cadence for Dedicated vs private? We need an outline to show finance.
43:30 Maya Chen: We'll send a pricing summary — Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly or annual commit tiers; Private has platform licensing plus deployment costs. I'll attach a one-pager.

44:20 Carlos Ruiz: Last technical note: when we recommend kernel maps, it's a suggested starting point. We still run microbenchmarks on your actual traffic before finalizing the runbook because op shapes can differ.
44:50 Leila Morgan: Ok that makes sense.

46:00 Maya Chen: Quick recap — we'll: 1) send the bench spreadsheet and prompt set, 2) provision a test tenant and run a 3-model bench, 3) output runbook and kernel mapping, 4) schedule pilot kickoff.
46:30 Amira Patel: Agreed. Please include the security docs and the compliance mapping.
46:50 Maya Chen: Will do. Carlos, any final technical notes?
47:05 Carlos Ruiz: Nothing new — I'll start provisioning and post access instructions. Expect the bench results by 4/10 and pilot kickoff proposed for 4/20.
47:25 Jon Reeves: Thanks all.
47:40 Leila Morgan: Thanks, this was helpful.
47:55 Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email with the artifacts and next steps.
48:10 (call ends)
